title: Freedom of Assembly and Cannabis Social Clubs

content_html_sanitized:
I was living in Dallas in the Summer of 1992 when it was announced that I would be the next National Director of NORML. As Monty Python used to say, “And now for something completely different.”

 

For the first time in my life I had my picture taken for publication. And for the only time in my life a Dallas newspaper published something about me. However, that led to my being invited to meet with a small group that had the courage to publicly oppose marijuana prohibition in a very Prohibitionist city.

 

At the appointed time, I found the small group in a dimly lit room, so we just sat around and talked. However, one of the young men said something that I will never forget. He thanked me for coming, because, “For the longest time, I thought that I was the only one who thought this way.”

 

Of course, this was just before a little thing called the “Internet” made it possible to circumvent the newspapers and local television stations keeping us isolated. However, it is still important for us to be able to “Assemble” in person.

 

The First Amendment of the United States Constitution protects not only the freedom of speech, but also the freedom of assembly, to meet together peacefully.

 

After I got to NORML I found that it still had more immediate relevance. Sometimes when NORML activists would announce that they were having a rally on their town square, they were told by the local constabulary that they would be arrested if they did.

 

They would then call the NORML office in D.C. We would then call the ACLU, who would call the town’s attorney, who would then call the sheriff, who would then announce that he would arrest anyone who actually had any weed.

 

That can still happen today, because cannabis possession is still illegal in half of the states.

See

Cannabis and Democracy: Who Are Our Leaders Following? It Ain't Us!

 

In this context, especially when possession is illegal, keeping cannabis users from sharing, the sharing becomes a secular sacrament. Freedom is always sacred.

 

Fifty years ago, when Henk de Vries opened The Bulldog, the first coffee shop in Amsterdam, he made the decision to have chairs and tables, and not just be a takeout, which would certainly have been a lot easier.

 

Several decades later, some enterprising cannabis aficionados in Barcelona decided to open venues for selling cannabis to the city’s enormous tourist traffic, and they called them “cannabis social clubs.” They are gone but the term has taken on a new meaning, especially in Germany, where “cannabis social clubs” are actually legal clubs. Incremental freedom is better than nothing.

 

However, the problem with these clubs is that, unlike coffee shops, they exclude the public.

See

Cannabis Retail Outlets: What’s In A Name? What Is The Best Model?

 

Cannabis prohibition actually created the culture surrounding the plant. If they had not arrested tens of millions of otherwise law abiding citizens, if they had not lied about an agricultural staple, and if they had not suppressed the medical use a traditional medicine and caused the unnecessary deaths and suffering of so many, then we could be happy just to meet and say, “Cheers!”. But, hell no!

 

I have joked that there’s a lot more smoke than sex in closets these days. It’s not just that we need to be “Out and Proud.” Of course we do. We also need to be “outspoken” until the people everywhere are free. Then we can have exclusive private clubs and exclude Prohibitionists riffraff.
